practice.title: Cultivate Superior Intention
agreedSteps: Cultivate superior intention — the thought 'I myself will liberate all living beings'
Examine your non-Dharma activities: what need are they filling, and could you fill it in a more virtuous way?
Try the split-screen visualization — imagine beings from all realms watching your actions and asking, 'Is that helping us?'
steps: Attune to the world of cause and effect — notice that every action, even small ones, has definite consequences
Reflect on the four general characteristics of karma: results are definite, results increase, if an action is not performed its result cannot be experienced, and actions are never wasted
Consider: what are the consequences of my lack of enlightenment? What suffering follows from my not yet being a Buddha?
practice.quote: I need to find a fire in me. It's not enough to just have a comfy club.

commentary.title: Exercising the Savior
content: We have to exercise the thought that someone else is going to come and do the heavy lifting — exercise it like getting a demon out, not like a workout. This idea that some great politician, thinker, or tech person is going to come solve everything — or even that Buddha is going to come back and do it — is a terrible thought. What we're really saying is: I can't be bothered to figure it out, and I'm not going to be the one to be of any help.

From a profound point of view, until we purify our own mind, we'll perceive a suffering world. So there's literally no way another person can solve it all, because we would still keep perceiving everything as suffering and full of misery. From one point of view, that person already came and freed everyone. The conclusion we need to reach is: No. Capital N, capital O, period. I have to take responsibility. It's no one else's. It's my job.
commentary.quote: There is no other person, actually. But from a profound point of view, right, until we purify our mind, we'll perceive a suffering world.

commentary.title: Energy and Vision
content: People have a lot of low-energy problems in this world, and it's because there's no spiritual vision for their life or the world. When we have a spiritual vision for our life and our world, we get a ton of energy — surging, actually, with energy. But people are disconnected from any spiritual vision, so there's no energy to do anything. Superior intention provides that vision.

commentary.title: Breaking Inner Conflict
content: One of the beautiful things about superior intention is that we stop being conflicted. The sense of going one way while wanting to go another is a dissonant, frictional feeling. It can lead to feeling like a fraud or a phony, and it gets in the way of helping anyone. But when we think 'I myself will do this,' we get completely crystal clear and focused. Our mind aligns. It's a very resonant and harmonious feeling inside — we're completely aligned with our values.

This is also a completely egoless state, even though from an ordinary point of view it looks like a huge ego. The paradox is worth pondering: how can we say 'I myself will liberate all living beings' without increasing self-grasping? The answer is that it's a mind essentially free of self-grasping — the mechanics of getting enlightened require extracting all self-cherishing, so there's no room for ordinary ego.

commentary.title: The Bodhisattva on the Scene
content: Imagine you're on a plane and they ask, 'Is anyone here a doctor?' It doesn't matter if you're a medical student or a surgeon — you have to respond. In each of our samsaras, we're the Bodhisattva on the scene. Nobody else is appearing. We can't say, 'Is there nobody else who can do it?' or 'I feel kind of tired today.' We just step in.

The overwhelm of trying to care for even a handful of people is actually a useful teaching. Ordinary me isn't the one who's going to liberate all living beings — that's impossible. I can't even liberate three or seven living beings with ordinary me. But we do have another alternative: imputing ourself correctly on Buddha Heruka or Vajrayogini. It's enlightened us that's going to actually do it.

commentary.title: Living in Cause and Effect
content: Another reason people have no energy is because they don't feel like their actions matter. They push paper, have meetings, watch shows — and it all just doesn't matter. Buddhism is based in a world of cause and effect, where every action really matters a lot and there are consequences to everything we do.

Working in the physical world is actually very grounding for this understanding. If you're building something and you mess it up, it falls and breaks. You can't just throw words at it. You're attuning to cause and effect in a direct way. Buddha used the analogy of gardening for the same reason — but these days we're so in a digital, separated world that we're out of touch with causes and effects.

commentary.title: Four Characteristics of Karma
content: The results of actions are definite — there's no fudging it. If a building is built badly, it falls. You can say 'I tried my best,' but there are just corpses there. It doesn't change what happened. The world of karma is like this: if the action was negative, it will have negative effects. It's a law. What would it be like to really see our spiritual practice like building a palace for all living beings?

The results of actions increase — karma is exponential, not like putting a penny in a piggy bank. One seed grows, makes more seeds, they grow and make more seeds. People planted invasive species at the temple years ago and thousands of hours have been spent trying to rip them out. That's karma too. Our positive actions, when dedicated, keep growing and increasing. Negative actions, if we don't purify them, grow and increase.

If an action is not performed, its result cannot be experienced. And an action is never wasted — we never get away with anything, good or bad. It always has an effect unless it's purified. Every action is like forever in the ledger of our mind stream.

commentary.title: Four Effects of Actions
content: Every single action creates four effects: a ripened effect (the realm we're reborn in), an environmental effect (the texture of that realm), an experience similar to the cause (how we experience the world), and a tendency similar to the cause (our behavior patterns). Every single tiny action creates an entire rebirth.

The environment is a mental experience, not an outer thing. Some people experience Brooklyn as scary, others as a dream come true. You can't change the environment you perceive except by changing your mind. And one action of love can create a reality of love — a whole world pervaded by love and peace. That's amazing.

commentary.title: Karma Feeds Superior Intention
content: At the level of superior intention, we're pondering that our not being enlightened has consequences. There are countless living beings drowning in the ocean of samsara that we're not helping. Those are effects — consequences of our lack of Buddhahood. Not being able to do something is an action. It's basically neglect.

This isn't about guilt — guilt is a selfish, self-cherishing mind. It's about taking responsibility and being courageous. The Buddhist center isn't a comfy club with nice people — it's about liberating all living beings. We want to have an outreach mindset: I need to protect the people of Brooklyn, and the world, and the people in hell, and the hungry ghosts, and the animals. I need to find a fire in me.
